title: Serving Runtime: Consolidated Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbook Playbook
author: Priya Raman
summary: Consolidated reference covering serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling playbooks, benchmark suite usage, runbooks for common incidents, known issues, and release notes. Intended as the canonical team wiki page for on-call engineers and runtime maintainers.
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime guidance used by the runtime, infra and performance teams. It includes: a high-level architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, step-by-step profiling and benchmarking playbooks, operational runbooks for common incidents, a curated list of known issues and workarounds, and release notes for recent runtime releases. Use this page as the single source of truth for runtime behavior and on-call procedures.

1) Runtime architecture (high-level)

- Purpose: provide a low-latency, high-throughput inference runtime for text generation, chat, embeddings and reranking workloads across hosted, dedicated and private deployments.
- Core components:
  - Frontend API layer (route, auth, request validation)
  - Router/scheduler: smart-routing based on policy (latency SLO, cost target, region, model-compatibility)
  - Execution pool: groups of GPUs/instances with allocation metadata (pool_id, hw_profile, quant_profile)
  - Serving runtime engine: kernel selection, KV cache, attention optimizations, batching layer, quantization backends
  - Cache layers: prefix cache (request prefixes), model weights cache, tokenized prompt cache (TTL configurable)
  - Telemetry & observability: per-token traces, request-level spans, per-route SLO metrics, cost accounting

- Design constraints and guarantees:
  - Latency SLOs: p50/p95/p99 targets are defined per-customer class (see "SLO table" below).
  - Graceful degradation: automatic fallback to compatible model variant or lower-precision quantized profile when capacity constrained.
  - Backpressure: admission control at the router to maintain latency SLOs under bursty load.

SLO table (examples):
| Customer tier | p95 latency (single-token) | throughput target | availability SLO |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Self-serve | 300ms | 200 rps per pool | 99.5% |
| Dedicated | 120ms | 1000 rps per pool | 99.9% |
| Enterprise (SLA) | 80ms | contractual | 99.95% |

2) Kernel scheduling architecture

Goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization while meeting latency SLOs.
- Minimize per-token cost via batching and efficient kernel selection.
- Avoid head-of-line latency amplification across heterogeneous models and sequence lengths.

Key concepts:
- Scheduling domain: Each execution pool maintains multiple scheduling domains partitioned by hardware capability (e.g., A100-80GB-int8, H100-80GB-fp16) and quantization profile.
- Work queues: Prioritized queues exist per scheduling domain and per route. Priority is computed from SLA, request age, and cost tier.
- Continuous batching: The scheduler forms micro-batches on-the-fly with a short wait budget (configurable, default 3ms) and max batch size per model/hw.
- Kernel chooser: Given model architecture, sequence-length distribution and current batch shape the kernel chooser selects the optimized kernel variant (fused attention, flash-attention, tiled attention, or custom fused kernels).
- Preemptive eviction: Long-running or background batched jobs can be preempted to serve high-priority single-token requests when latency budgets are tight.

Kernel scheduling knobs (config table):
| knob | default | description | owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| batch_wait_budget_ms | "3" | Max time scheduler waits to form a batch | serving-runtime |
| max_batch_size_per_model | "64" | Max batch dimension for model family | model-onboarding |
| kernel_selection_policy | "latency-first" | Options: latency-first, throughput-first, cost-first | serving-runtime |
| preemption_threshold_ms | "50" | If head request latency projection > threshold, preempt background batches | serving-runtime |

3) Profiling & diagnostic playbook (step-by-step)

Purpose: Provide a reproducible workflow for diagnosing slowness, tail latency, or throughput regressions.

Preconditions: access to the runtime dev cluster, profiling artifacts bucket, and trace viewer.

Procedure:
1. Verify scope and reproducibility:
   a. Confirm the incident window and affected routes/customers.
   b. Reproduce with a synthetic load (use the benchmark harness) targeting the same model, prompt length distribution and concurrency.
2. Collect telemetry:
   - Enable detailed per-request span collection for the test run (sample rate 100% for diagnosis).
   - Capture GPU metrics (utilization, SM occupancy, tensor core activity), PCIe counters and NVLink bandwidth for the period.
   - Dump kernel-level timelines from the runtime (start/end per-kernel).
3. Run profiler tools:
   - CPU-side: perf, eBPF-based top-like traces for system calls.
   - GPU-side: nsight systems for full timeline and nvprof for kernel-level hotspots.
   - Runtime: enable kernel timing logs (log level DEBUG_PROFILING).
4. Analyze hot paths:
   - Identify unusually slow kernels (long-tail); correlate with batch shapes and sequence lengths.
   - Check scheduling queues for head-of-line blocking or long queue residency.
   - Confirm KV cache hit/miss for affected prefixes.
5. Hypothesis and test:
   - If kernel is inefficient for observed shape, test alternate kernel variant via runtime flag --kernel-override=<variant>.
   - If batching wait budget causes latency tails, reduce batch_wait_budget_ms to 1-2ms and re-evaluate.
   - If GPU SM occupancy is low, tune fusion/build flags; consider different kernel binary.
6. Implement mitigation and monitor:
   - Temporary mitigations: route-weighted throttling, route fallback to lower-precision model, or pin requests to a dedicated low-latency pool.
   - Post-mitigation: run 30m stability run and validate latency SLOs and utilization.

Common diagnostic commands (examples):
- Synthetic load: ./bench/harness --model gpt-3k --concurrency 200 --prompt-dist prompts/short_and_long.json
- Collect GPU usage: nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 2 
- Nsight capture: nsys profile --output=trace.nsys --target-processes=all --duration=60s --trace=nvtx

4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration

What to measure:
- Per-token latency (p50/p95/p99) across realistic prompt length distributions.
- Throughput at SLO constraint (max sustained rps while meeting p95 target).
- Cost per token estimates across quantization profiles and batching configs.
- Memory overhead and KV cache hit ratio.

Benchmark harness components:
- bench/harness: driver that runs synthetic user workloads (supports multi-route, multi-tenant mix).
- bench/configs/: workload definitions (short-chat, long-doc-gen, embeddings-bulk).
- bench/reporter: collects telemetry and emits standardized JSON artifacts stored in s3://redwood-perf/artifacts/{run_id}/

CI gating:
- Nightly perf job runs benchmark suites against the canary cluster and compares results to a baseline run. Thresholds are defined per-metric (regression if p95 increases by >5% or throughput drops by >3%).
- On PR: lightweight microbench that validates no catastrophic regression for touched kernels (5 runs, 95th percentile check).

Interpreting artifacts:
- artifact.json contains typed metrics with fields: run_id, model, hw_profile, batch_config, p50, p95, p99, throughput, cost_per_token_usd (note: these artifacts are JSON files inside the artifacts bucket; use bench/reporter to parse).

5) Operational runbooks (common incidents)

Runbook: High p95 latency on production route
1. Scope: identify affected route(s) and time window.
2. Quick triage (first 10 minutes):
   - Check route-level dashboards: p50/p95/p99 latency, queue lengths, per-pool GPU utilization.
   - If route has automatic fallback enabled, confirm whether fallback has triggered.
3. Immediate mitigations (choose one):
   - Reduce concurrency by applying temporary rate-limit to route in router (preferred for burst).
   - Increase pool capacity (if autoscaler has capacity and spin-up time acceptable).
   - Fallback route to quantized model variant or pinned low-latency pool.
4. Diagnostic steps: follow profiling playbook to gather logs and traces.
5. Post-incident: add replay job to reproduce at scale and capture artifacts for root cause.

Runbook: GPU OOM on pool
1. Identify the job/pod that OOMed and the model/quant-profile in use.
2. Immediate mitigation: restart pod with conservative memory soft-limits and enable spill-to-host for KV cache.
3. If OOM reproducible, reduce max_batch_size_per_model for that model family and mark for model-onboarding review.

6) Known issues and workarounds (current list)
- Kernel fallback on H100 (issue #1423): under certain batch shapes, the fp16 fused kernel may return non-deterministic outputs for extremely long sequences (>16k tokens). Workaround: force use of tiled-attention kernel (--kernel-override=tiled) until fixed.
- NVLink peer-to-peer stall (issue #1560): rare stalls during cross-GPU KV sync. Workaround: enable KV sync batching (env KV_SYNC_BATCH_MS=5) or pin large-prefix workloads to single GPU.
- Batch packing misalignment after model upgrade (issue #1602): older micro-batch heuristics lead to suboptimal batch shapes. Workaround: clear runtime batch caches and restart pool after rolling upgrade.

7) Recent release notes (summary)
- 2026-02-15 (v2026.02.15): kernel chooser upgraded to include heuristic for sequence-length-aware fusion; default batch_wait_budget_ms reduced from 5ms to 3ms.
- 2025-12-01 (v2025.12.01): introduce KV sync batching for NVLink (experimental flag).
- 2025-08-18 (v2025.08.18): added preemption for background batch jobs; improved admission-control thresholds.

8) Team wiki & onboarding pointers
- Quickstart: bench/README.md (how to run harness locally).
- Kernel dev guide: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-dev.md
- Profiling artifacts: s3://redwood-perf/artifacts/ (standardized layout).
- Pager rotation: oncall/rota/serving-runtime (contact list and escalation path).

9) Ownership, escalation and contacts
- Primary owner: serving-runtime team (team alias: eng-serving-runtime@redwood.com)
- Oncall: listed in team wiki page; escalate to infra-sre for hardware incidents, and to model-onboarding for model-specific regressions.
- Pager escalation matrix:
  - 0-15m: oncall engineer (attempt mitigation)
  - 15-45m: oncall + tech lead (apply mitigations, consider capacity scale)
  - 45m+: paging manager and infra-sre (executes cross-team mitigations)

Appendix A: Recommended tuning defaults
- batch_wait_budget_ms = 3
- max_batch_size_per_model = 64
- kernel_selection_policy = latency-first
- preemption_threshold_ms = 50
- kv_cache_ttl_seconds = 300

Appendix B: Example CLI snippets
- Run a profiling harness run and upload artifacts:
  ./bench/harness --workload short-chat --concurrency 300 --duration 300 --collect-profiling --output s3://redwood-perf/artifacts/$RUN_ID/

- Force kernel variant for a test run:
  RUNTIME_FLAGS=--kernel-override=flash-attn ./runtime/serve --pool-id=test-pool --model gpt-4x

Appendix C: Document maintenance
- Owner should review this doc quarterly or after any major runtime release.
- If you update kernel defaults or add a new knob, add a change note with date and PR link below the release notes section.

End of document.
